title: Tale of the Man Who Was Lavish

keywords: tale of the man who was lavish
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived an affluent merchant named Mansur who was celebrated for his open-handed hospitality. For thirty years, his doors stood open to travelers, he paid the debts of bankrupt craftsmen, and provided dowries for the daughters of impoverished widows, never asking for repayment.

A disastrous fire swept through the harbor, destroying Mansur’s warehouses, his ships, and his home, leaving the noble elder without a single silver dirham.

Mansur sat upon the steps of the Great Mosque, his head bowed, preparing to endure his poverty with silent dignity.

Word of his misfortune spread through the bazaars of Basra.

Within three hours, an extraordinary sight was seen: hundreds of citizens—bakers, carpenters, weavers, fishermen, and wealthy merchants—gathered in the square!

Each brought what he could: the wealthy merchants brought bags of gold; the weavers brought bolts of cloth; the carpenters brought timber and tools; and the poor laborers brought their copper coins, saying: 'When we were in despair, Mansur’s hand lifted us up; today, the city shall rebuild Mansur’s house!'

Before sunset, Mansur stood surrounded by thirty thousand dinars, his warehouses were rebuilt by volunteer labor, and his ships were restored by the shipbuilders guild!

Mansur wept with joyful gratitude, learning that the gold you hoard in iron vaults is lost in an hour, but the generosity you invest in the hearts of your community is an eternal fortress that no fire can ever destroy.
moral: Bread cast upon the waters of hospitality returns as an unbreakable fortress of community support.
